title: Can ChatGPT give feedback?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou asks whether ChatGPT can give students useful written feedback and concludes that the question is partly the wrong one. Using a driving-instructor analogy, she argues that delayed, mark-scheme-style written comments, whether from a human or a bot, are less helpful than in-the-moment guidance or targeted correction. That is why she values whole-class feedback, where teachers read the work and replan the next lesson, as both faster and more effective than traditional comments. She suggests that ChatGPT's mark-scheme comments may only serve the bureaucratic side of marking, and warns against excitement about generated comments undoing genuine improvements. Her closing move is to note that people tend to use new technology to replicate the old, and to ask whether the tool could instead produce individualized feedback closer to whole-class feedback. Close call: the AI tool is the explicit subject, so it is placed in Ed-Tech rather than Learning & Curriculum.
points: Written comments linked to a mark scheme are of limited help to students, regardless of whether a human or ChatGPT writes them.
The driving-instructor analogy shows that feedback tied to the moment of performance is more useful than a letter arriving a week later.
Whole-class feedback saves time and is also more effective, so time-saving does not imply a cheaper outcome.
ChatGPT comments may fit the performative, box-ticking side of marking, freeing teachers to give feedback that matters.
Replicating old practice with a new technology wastes it; the better question is whether AI can do something different and more specific.
quotes: It can also provide written feedback, which has got everyone excited about the potential time savings. If you give ChatGPT the mark scheme and ask it to give the essay a grade and explain why, it can produce a comment that uses the language of the mark scheme.
Which kind of feedback is more useful? The first, obviously. Which kind of feedback is more time consuming for the instructor? The second, obviously.

And this is why one of the most interesting innovations in English education in recent years has been the development of whole-class feedback. The principle behind whole-class feedback is that instead of a teacher spending hours writing out comments like the above, they read their students’ writing and replan their next lesson based on the strengths and weaknesses they have seen.
Whole-class feedback saves time, but that is not the only rationale for it. It is more effective than traditional written comments.

So is there any point in using ChatGPT’s mark-scheme based written comments? Perhaps they could fulfil the performative aspect of marking. A detailed comment that is linked to the mark scheme will tick a lot of bureaucratic boxes, and the teacher can get on with actually teaching and feeding back to students in a way that is useful.

I hope that whole-class feedback will continue. It is a far more effective innovation than the comment above, and I would hate to see the genuine pedagogical improvements brought about by whole-class feedback set back because people get starry-eyed about automatically generated text comments.

However, ChatGPT’s language abilities are undeniably impressive. And in fact, by trying to get it to replicate the traditional mark-scheme based written comment, perhaps we are missing a trick. We’re doing that thing everyone does when a new technology comes along, which is to use it in exactly the way we used the old one — eg, bosses who got their secretaries to print out all their emails and then dictated responses to them.
